channel.title: Pharm Final — The forecast
channel.description: Joan’s 11 short answers sit under three clinical scenarios, so this episode opens with three forecast scenarios built the way her formative mini-exams are, using the drugs she named: paracetamol and salbutamol (her exam-prep slides: “medications with specific questions”), the anticoagulants, GTN, beta blockers, the penicillins and morphine. Then a track for each of those drugs, every module on her exam list, and her own formative keys. Every answer is a definition plus an example, about two lines a mark, the way she asked. The final: Thu 5 Nov · 30 multi-choice + 11 short answers (1–4 marks, under 3 scenarios) · 80 min · 50%.

item.title: 01 · How this forecast works
item.description: Joan’s 11 short answers sit under three clinical scenarios, so this episode opens with three forecast scenarios built the way her formative mini-exams are, using the drugs she named: paracetamol and salbutamol (her exam-prep slides: “medications with specific questions”), the anticoagulants, GTN, beta blockers, the penicillins and morphine. Then a track for each of those drugs, every module on her exam list, and her own formative keys. Every answer is a definition plus an example, about two lines a mark, the way she asked.

item.title: 02 · Scenario 1: Mrs Harris, asthma and atrial fibrillation
item.description: What drug class is salbutamol, and how does it work? Identify two assessments the nurse makes before and after Mrs Harris uses her salbutamol. Warfarin is an anticoagulant. Identify one test used to monitor it and one sign of bleeding to teach her to report. Define polypharmacy and give one strategy to support Mrs Harris with her medicines. Identify one age-related change that may mean Mrs Harris needs a lower dose.

item.title: 03 · Scenario 2: Leo, four, with an ear infection
item.description: Calculate Leo's single dose of paracetamol. Identify two reasons Leo is given paracetamol. Why are children prescribed lower doses than adults? Ana says Leo might be "a bit allergic" to antibiotics. What should the nurse do, and what is an allergic reaction? Give one piece of safe advice for Ana about storing and giving amoxicillin suspension.

item.title: 04 · Scenario 3: Mr Tane, after surgery, with angina
item.description: Morphine is a controlled drug. What is a controlled drug, and give one way it is handled differently on the ward? Identify two things the nurse monitors after giving Mr Tane morphine. Why is GTN given sublingually, and what is one side effect? Mr Tane says he doesn't want his next dose. What should the nurse do?

item.title: 05 · Paracetamol
item.description: Describe paracetamol: its class, what it is used for, and one important nursing consideration.

item.title: 06 · Salbutamol
item.description: Describe salbutamol: its class, how it works, and what the nurse teaches about using it.

item.title: 07 · Aspirin, warfarin and heparin
item.description: Compare an antiplatelet with an anticoagulant, giving an example of each, and identify one nursing consideration for warfarin.

item.title: 08 · Beta blockers and GTN
item.description: Explain how a beta blocker works, and identify what the nurse checks before giving one. Describe GTN: its class, why it is sublingual, and what to teach.

item.title: 09 · The penicillins and antimicrobials
item.description: Why does Joan call them antimicrobials rather than antibiotics? Give one nursing consideration before giving a penicillin.

item.title: 10 · Morphine and the opioids
item.description: Describe morphine's class and identify two adverse effects the nurse monitors for.

item.title: 11 · Pharmacokinetics
item.description: Name and describe the four processes of pharmacokinetics that an oral medicine goes through.

item.title: 12 · Pharmacodynamics and drug effects
item.description: Define an agonist and an antagonist, with an example of each. Define a side effect and an adverse drug reaction, with an example.

item.title: 13 · Drug names, the law and who's who
item.description: Medicines have a chemical, a generic and a brand name. Which is most important for the RN to use, and why? Choose one legal classification of medicines and describe how a patient gets it.

item.title: 14 · Giving medicines safely
item.description: Identify one of the rights of medication administration and give an example of how it is applied in aged care.

item.title: 15 · Abbreviations
item.description: Interpret the abbreviations on a medication chart. (about 5 marks across the paper)

item.title: 16 · Calculations
item.description: Her formative calculations (1 mark each)

item.title: 17 · Medicines across the lifespan
item.description: Describe the function of the placental barrier and define a teratogenic effect.

item.title: 18 · Allergy, anaphylaxis and vaccines
item.description: Identify two symptoms of anaphylaxis the nurse monitors for after a vaccination, and describe the first-line treatment.

item.title: 19 · Licit and illicit drugs, dependence and addiction
item.description: Define drug dependence and drug addiction, and explain the difference, with an example.

item.title: 20 · Adherence and the cost of medicines
item.description: Define medication adherence and list four barriers that may stop a patient achieving it. (5 marks over two questions)

item.title: 21 · Complementary medicine and rongoā Māori
item.description: Define complementary and alternative medicine, with an example of each, and describe the nurse's response when a patient plans to stop their treatment for an alternative.

item.title: 22 · Drug development and research ethics
item.description: Identify and describe one ethical consideration of a patient taking part in a clinical trial.

item.title: 23 · The multi-choice: her keys and the classes both ways
item.description: Her formative keys and class definitions (1 mark each)
